content: There is no universally agreed-upon standard for what constitutes a normal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) level. A threshold of 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) has been proposed by some experts. However, it is a common misconception that the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) serves as a strict cutoff point, implying that nearly the entire population must maintain serum 25(OH)D levels above 20 ng/mL to ensure optimal bone health. In reality, only about 5% of the population requires levels of 20 ng/mL or less to meet their needs. Furthermore, based on the definition of an average requirement, approximately half of the population has a requirement of 16 ng/mL (the Estimated Average Requirement, or EAR) or less. The definition of vitamin D deficiency can also be determined by the point at which parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels plateau, which may occur at a serum 25(OH)D level of 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) or closer to 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L). According to the Institute of Medicine (IOM): Serum 25(OH)D levels above 20 ng/mL are considered sufficient for practically all persons. Levels between 12 and 20 ng/mL (less than 50 nmol/L) indicate that some, but not all, individuals may be at risk for inadequacy. Levels below 12 ng/mL (less than 30 nmol/L) place individuals at risk of vitamin D deficiency.
